questions.question: What are the names of the five Sikhs initiated by Guru Gobind Singh Ji to form the Khalsa?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Panj Pyare**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Panj Pyare** (literally meaning the **Five Beloved Ones**) were the five individuals who responded to **Guru Gobind Singh Ji**'s call for sacrifice on the day of **Vaisakhi** in **1699** at **Anandpur Sahib**.
 
• These five brave men were **Bhai Daya Singh** (a Khatri from Lahore), **Bhai Dharam Singh** (a Jat from Hastinapur), **Bhai Himmat Singh** (a water-carrier from Jagannath Puri), **Bhai Mohkam Singh** (a tailor from Dwarka), and **Bhai Sahib Singh** (a barber from Bidar).
 
• The selection of these individuals from different castes and different parts of the Indian subcontinent was a deliberate act by **Guru Gobind Singh Ji** to abolish the **Caste System** and promote universal brotherhood.
 
• They were the first to receive **Khande di Pahul** (initiation with a double-edged sword) and formed the nucleus of the **Khalsa Panth**, a community of saint-soldiers dedicated to righteousness and protection of the oppressed.
 
• After initiating them, **Guru Gobind Singh Ji** himself received initiation from the **Panj Pyare**, establishing the principle of **Aape Gur Chela** (the Guru is the Disciple and the Disciple is the Guru).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **The Khalsa Identity**:

 
 
• **The Five Ks**: The **Panj Pyare** were the first to adopt the five mandatory articles of faith: **Kesh** (uncut hair), **Kangha** (wooden comb), **Kara** (iron bracelet), **Kachera** (cotton undergarments), and **Kirpan** (ceremonial sword).
 
• **Titles**: To further eliminate social hierarchy, all initiated men were given the title **Singh** (meaning Lion) and women were given the title **Kaur** (meaning Princess or Lioness).
 
• **Rehit Maryada**: The **Panj Pyare** were entrusted with upholding the **Code of Conduct** (Rehit) and have the authority to lead the community in religious and administrative matters through **Gurmattas** (collective resolutions).
 
• **Amrit Sanchar**: The initiation ceremony involved stirring sugar crystals (Patashas) in water with a **Khanda** while reciting the five prayers: **Japji Sahib**, **Jaap Sahib**, **Tav-Prasad Savaiye**, **Chaupai Sahib**, and **Anand Sahib**.

questions.question: Just before an object strikes the ground during free fall (ignoring air resistance), how are its potential and kinetic energies related?

options.text: Potential energy is maximum, kinetic energy is minimum
Potential energy is minimum, kinetic energy is maximum
Both kinetic and potential energies are zero
Some energy is lost due to transformation

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Potential energy is minimum, kinetic energy is maximum**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• According to the **Law of Conservation of Energy**, energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be transformed from one form to another. In a **free-fall** scenario where **air resistance** is neglected, the total **mechanical energy** (sum of potential and kinetic energy) remains constant.
 
• **Potential Energy (PE)** is defined as **mgh**, where **m** is mass, **g** is acceleration due to gravity, and **h** is the height above the reference level. As the object falls, its **height** decreases, causing the **potential energy** to decrease until it reaches its **minimum value** (zero) just before striking the ground.
 
• **Kinetic Energy (KE)** is defined as **1/2 mv²**, where **v** is the velocity. During the fall, the force of **gravity** accelerates the object, causing its **velocity** to increase continuously.
 
• Just before the impact, the object reaches its **terminal velocity** for that specific height, making the **Kinetic Energy** reach its **maximum value**. At this point, nearly all the initial potential energy has been converted into kinetic energy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mechanical Energy Components**:

 
 
• **Gravitational Potential Energy**: This is highest at the **maximum altitude** and lowest at **ground level**. It depends directly on the vertical displacement from the **datum line**.
 
• **Kinetic Energy**: This is zero when the object is at **rest** (at the start of the fall) and reaches its peak just before the object is stopped by the **ground**.
 
• **Energy Transformation**: While the object is in motion, there is a continuous **interconversion** between PE and KE, but their sum stays the same if **non-conservative forces** (like friction) are absent.
 
 
 
• **Invalid Scenarios**:
 
 
• **Energy Loss**: In an ideal physics problem ignoring **air resistance**, no energy is lost to **heat** or **sound** during the fall itself; transformation only occurs upon **impact**.
 
• **Zero Energy**: The kinetic energy cannot be zero at the point of impact as the object possesses **maximum velocity**.

questions.question: Who is the author of Interpreter of Maladies?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Jhumpa Lahiri**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Jhumpa Lahiri** is the author of the acclaimed debut short story collection titled **Interpreter of Maladies**, which was published in **1999**.
 
• The book is a collection of **nine distinct stories** that explore the lives of **Indians** and **Indian Americans** who are caught between their traditional roots and the complexities of the **New World**.
 
• In **2000**, the collection was awarded the **Pulitzer Prize for Fiction**, making **Lahiri** one of the youngest authors to receive this prestigious honor.
 
• The stories frequently address themes of **cultural isolation**, the immigrant experience, **marital friction**, and the search for identity in **post-colonial** contexts.
 
• Notable stories within the collection include **A Temporary Matter**, **The Treatment of Bibi Haldar**, and the title story **Interpreter of Maladies**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Arundhati Roy**

 
 
• She is an influential Indian author best known for her debut novel, **The God of Small Things**, which won the **Man Booker Prize** in **1997**.
 
• Her work is characterized by its exploration of **caste dynamics**, family relationships, and **political activism** in India.
 
 
 
• **Kiran Desai**
 
 
• She is the author of **The Inheritance of Loss**, which won the **Man Booker Prize** in **2006**.
 
• Her narratives often deal with **globalization**, **colonialism**, and the migration between the **East and the West**.
 
 
 
• **Anita Desai**
 
 
• A prolific Indian novelist and mother of Kiran Desai, she has been shortlisted for the **Booker Prize** three times for novels such as **Clear Light of Day** and **In Custody**.
 
• She was honored with the **Sahitya Akademi Award** in **1978** and the **Padma Bhushan** in **2014**.

questions.question: Which of the following rivers forms the world's largest delta?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ganga-Brahmaputra**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Ganga-Brahmaputra Delta**, also famously known as the **Sunderbans Delta** or the **Bengal Delta**, is the **largest delta in the world**.
 
• It is situated in the **South Asian** region, covering a vast area of approximately **105,000 square kilometers** across **Bangladesh** and the **Indian state of West Bengal**.
 
• This **arcuate (fan-shaped)** delta is formed by the confluence of three major river systems: the **Ganga**, the **Brahmaputra**, and the **Meghna**, which eventually drain into the **Bay of Bengal**.
 
• The region is exceptionally **fertile** due to the massive amount of **alluvial soil** deposited annually by these Himalayan rivers, earning it the nickname the **Green Delta**.
 
• It is home to the **Sundarbans**, which is the world’s largest contiguous **mangrove forest** and is designated as a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indus River**:

 
 
• Originates in the **Kailash Range** of **Tibet** and flows through **Ladakh** before entering **Pakistan**.
 
• It forms a significant delta near **Karachi** on the **Arabian Sea**, though it is much smaller and more **arid** than the Bengal Delta.
 
 
 
• **Godavari River**:
 
 
• Known as the **Dakshin Ganga**, it is the largest river in **Peninsular India**, originating from **Trimbakeshwar** in **Maharashtra**.
 
• It forms a **lobate delta** on the **East Coast** of India in **Andhra Pradesh**.
 
 
 
• **Krishna River**:
 
 
• Originates near **Mahabaleshwar** in the **Western Ghats** and is the second-largest east-flowing peninsular river.
 
• Its delta is located at **Hamsaladeevi** in **Andhra Pradesh** and is a vital region for **paddy cultivation**.

questions.question: If the satellite's orbital period is 90 minutes, what is the key force keeping it in orbit?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gravitational force of Earth**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Gravitational force of Earth** acts as the essential **centripetal force** required to keep a satellite in a stable circular or elliptical orbit. Without this constant inward pull, the satellite would fly off in a straight line into space due to its **inertia**.
 
• An orbital period of approximately **90 minutes** is a characteristic feature of a satellite in **Low Earth Orbit (LEO)**. To maintain this period, the satellite must travel at a very high tangential velocity of roughly **7.8 km/s** or **28,000 km/h**.
 
• At an altitude of about **200 to 400 kilometers**, the **acceleration due to gravity** is still approximately **90%** of its value at the Earth surface. The satellite remains in orbit because its **horizontal velocity** is so high that the curvature of its fall matches the **curvature of the Earth**.
 
• According to **Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation**, the force is proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centers. This force provides the **acceleration** ( v² / r ) necessary for circular motion.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Centrifugal force**:

 
 
• It is often mistaken as a real force, but it is actually a **pseudo-force** or inertial force experienced only within a **rotating reference frame**. It does not pull the satellite; rather, the satellite's inertia resists the change in direction caused by gravity.
 
 
 
• **Magnetic and Electromagnetic forces**:
 
 
• While the Earth possesses a **magnetic field** (magnetosphere), its primary role is to deflect **solar wind** and cosmic radiation. It is far too weak to provide the mechanical force needed to hold a massive satellite in its **orbital trajectory**.
 
• **Electromagnetic forces** are dominant at the atomic level or in specific propulsion technologies like **Hall-effect thrusters**, but they are not the primary drivers of **celestial mechanics** or orbital stability.

questions.question: If the Moon takes 27 days to orbit Earth, how many degrees does it move per day along its orbit?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**13.3degree**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Moon** moves around the **Earth** in a nearly circular path called a **revolution** or an **orbit**.
 
• In geometry and astronomy, a complete revolution or one full circle around a central body is defined as **360 degrees** of angular displacement.
 
• The time the **Moon** takes to complete one full orbit relative to the stars is its **sidereal period**, which is approximately **27.3 days**; however, for simplified mathematical problems, it is often rounded to **27 days**.
 
• To determine the daily angular speed of the **Moon**, the total degrees in the orbit (**360**) must be divided by the total number of days taken to complete that orbit (**27**).
 
• The calculation is expressed as: **360 ÷ 27 ≈ 13.333**. When rounded to one decimal place, this equals **13.3 degrees** per day.
 
• This eastward movement of approximately **13.3 degrees** every 24 hours explains why the **Moon** rises approximately **50 minutes later** each day.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Lunar Orbital Mechanics**:

 
 
• **Sidereal vs. Synodic Month**: While the **sidereal month** (the physical orbit) is **27.32 days**, the **synodic month** (the time between two New Moons) is **29.53 days** because the **Earth** also moves along its orbit around the **Sun** during that time.
 
• **Variable Speed**: The **Moon** follows an **elliptical orbit**. According to **Kepler’s Second Law**, it moves faster at **perigee** (closest point to Earth) and slower at **apogee** (farthest point).
 
• **Tidal Locking**: The **Moon** takes the same amount of time to rotate once on its axis as it does to orbit the **Earth** (**27.3 days**), which is why we always see the same lunar face.
 
 
 
• **Angular Observations**:
 
 
• The **angular diameter** of the **Moon** in the night sky is roughly **0.5 degrees**.
 
• Since the **Moon** moves **13.3 degrees** per day, it travels a distance in the sky roughly equal to its own diameter every **hour**.

questions.question: Which Indian satellite helped in monitoring cyclones like Hudhud and Phailin?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**INSAT-3D**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **INSAT-3D** is an advanced **meteorological satellite** developed by the **Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)**, launched on **July 26, 2013**.
 
• It was specifically designed for enhanced **meteorological observations** and monitoring of **land and ocean surfaces** to improve **weather forecasting** and **disaster warning** systems.
 
• The satellite proved instrumental in tracking **Cyclone Phailin** in **October 2013** and **Cyclone Hudhud** in **October 2014**, providing accurate data on **cyclone intensity** and **landfall predictions**.
 
• Equipped with a **6-channel Imager** and a **19-channel Sounder**, it allowed the **India Meteorological Department (IMD)** to obtain precise **vertical profiles of temperature** and **atmospheric humidity**.
 
• By providing **high-resolution imagery** every 30 minutes, **INSAT-3D** significantly reduced the uncertainty in **natural disaster** tracking in the **Bay of Bengal** and the **Arabian Sea**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Cartosat-1**:

 
 
• Launched in **2005**, it is the first **dedicated cartographic satellite** of India, providing **high-resolution stereo imagery** for **3D mapping** and **terrain modeling**.
 
 
 
• **GSAT-7**:
 
 
• Commonly known as **Rukmini**, it is a multi-band **military communication satellite** specifically built for the **Indian Navy** to provide secure **real-time communication** across the **Indian Ocean Region**.
 
 
 
• **RISAT-2**:
 
 
• A **Radar Imaging Satellite** launched in **2009**, it features **Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR)**, enabling **all-weather** and **day-night surveillance** for **border security** and **disaster management**.

questions.question: The Second Five-Year Plan (1956-61) focused primarily on
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Industrialization and heavy industries**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Second Five-Year Plan**, which operated from **1956 to 1961**, was primarily based on the **Mahalanobis Model**, named after the prominent Indian statistician **Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis**.
 
• The plan marked a strategic shift in India's development trajectory by prioritizing **rapid industrialization** over the agricultural focus of the First Plan.
 
• The central objective was the development of **basic and heavy industries**, such as **iron and steel**, **chemicals**, and **heavy engineering**, to create a self-reliant industrial base.
 
• During this period, three major **public sector steel plants** were established with international cooperation: **Bhilai** (with the help of the USSR), **Durgapur** (with the help of the UK), and **Rourkela** (with the help of West Germany).
 
• The plan also targeted a **25 percent increase** in the **national income** to improve the standard of living and foster economic growth.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mahalanobis Strategy**:

 
 
• This strategy emphasized investment in the **capital goods sector**, under the belief that producing machines that make other machines would accelerate the rate of **capital formation** and long-term economic independence.
 
 
 
• **Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956**:
 
 
• This resolution served as the economic blueprint for the Second Plan, aiming to establish a **socialistic pattern of society** where the **public sector** would hold the 'commanding heights' of the economy.
 
 
 
• **Technological and Scientific Advancements**:
 
 
• The **Atomic Energy Commission** was established in **1958** with **Homi J. Bhabha** as the first chairman, signifying the emphasis on modern scientific research during this era.
 
• Higher education and technical training were bolstered through the development of **Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs)** to provide the skilled workforce needed for large-scale industrial projects.
 
 
 
• **Other Institutional Developments**:
 
 
• The **Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC)** was established in **1957** to promote rural employment, showing that while heavy industry was the priority, **cottage industries** were still maintained for social balance.

questions.question: Who won India's only medal in athletics at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Neeraj Chopra**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Neeraj Chopra** created history by winning the **Gold Medal** in the **Men's Javelin Throw** at the **Tokyo 2020 Olympics** (held in 2021).
 
• He achieved a remarkable distance of **87.58 meters** in his second attempt during the final, securing the top position on the podium.
 
• This victory marked **India's first-ever Olympic gold medal in athletics** and the country's first athletics medal since independence.
 
• With this feat, he became the second Indian to win an **individual Olympic gold medal**, following **Abhinav Bindra**, who won gold in shooting at the **2008 Beijing Olympics**.
 
• His historic achievement ended a **121-year wait** for an Olympic medal in track and field for India, the previous ones being two silvers won by **Norman Pritchard** in 1900.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Anju Bobby George**:

 
 
• She is a legendary Indian **Long Jumper** who became the first Indian athlete to win a medal at the **World Championships in Athletics** (Bronze in 2003, Paris).
 
• She represented India at the **2004 Athens Olympics**, where she finished in the fifth position (later upgraded to fourth).
 
 
 
• **Avinash Sable**:
 
 
• An Indian track and field athlete specializing in the **3000 meters steeplechase** event.
 
• He holds multiple **National Records** and won the silver medal at the **2022 Commonwealth Games** in Birmingham.
 
 
 
• **Hima Das**:
 
 
• Nicknamed the **Dhing Express**, she is a sprinter from **Assam** specializing in 400m and 200m races.
 
• She was the first Indian athlete to win a gold medal in a track event at the **IAAF World U20 Championships** in 2018.

questions.question: Which international organization oversees the global fight against doping in sports?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**WADA**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA)** is the primary international organization established to coordinate and monitor the fight against drugs in sports.
 
• It was founded on **November 10, 1999**, in **Lausanne, Switzerland**, following the **First World Conference on Doping in Sport** and the subsequent **Declaration of Lausanne**.
 
• WADA is currently headquartered in **Montreal, Quebec, Canada**, since 2002.
 
• The agency is responsible for the **World Anti-Doping Code**, a comprehensive document that harmonizes anti-doping regulations across all sports and all countries.
 
• Its core activities include **scientific research**, **education**, and the development of **anti-doping capacities** to ensure a level playing field for all athletes globally.
 
• The organization is funded equally by the **Olympic Movement** and **governments** of the world, ensuring a balanced governance structure between sports bodies and public authorities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **IOC (International Olympic Committee)**:

 
 
• An independent non-profit international organization based in **Lausanne, Switzerland**, responsible for the **Olympic Games**.
 
• While it initiated the creation of WADA, its primary focus is the broader management of the **Olympic Movement**.
 
 
 
• **USADA (United States Anti-Doping Agency)**:
 
 
• The **national anti-doping organization (NADO)** specifically for the **United States**.
 
• It manages drug testing and results for U.S. athletes in **Olympic** and **Paralympic** sports but does not have global jurisdiction.
 
 
 
• **NADA (National Anti-Doping Agency)**:
 
 
• The national body responsible for monitoring and promoting anti-doping activities in **India**.
 
• It operates under the **Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports** and implements **WADA-compliant** policies within the Indian sporting ecosystem.

questions.concept: External Sector and Currency Exchange rate
questions.question: The trade policy of the 1950s-1980s in India emphasized:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Import substitution and protectionism**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• From **1950 to 1990**, India adopted an **inward-looking trade strategy**, officially known as **Import Substitution Industrialization (ISI)**, to achieve **self-reliance**.
 
• The primary goal was to replace imports with **domestic production**, ensuring that goods previously purchased from abroad were manufactured within the country to save **foreign exchange reserves**.
 
• The government protected **infant industries** from foreign competition using two main instruments: **tariffs** (high taxes on imported goods) and **quotas** (strict limits on the quantity of goods that could be imported).
 
• This policy framework was heavily influenced by the **Mahalanobis Model** during the **Second Five-Year Plan**, which prioritized the development of **heavy and capital goods industries**.
 
• Under the **Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956**, the state maintained supreme control over trade and industry, a system often referred to as the **License Raj**.
 
• The strategy successfully diversified India's industrial base into sectors like **electronics** and **automobiles**, which would have struggled to survive against established global competitors without **protectionism**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Economic Liberalization (1991)**:

 
 
• Following a severe **Balance of Payments (BoP) crisis** in **1991**, India shifted toward **Liberalization, Privatization, and Globalization (LPG)**.
 
• This reform era marked the end of the **License Raj** and moved the economy toward **export promotion** and **free trade**.
 
 
 
• **Foreign Portfolio Investment (FPI)**:
 
 
• FPI involves investing in **financial assets** such as stocks and bonds. This was largely restricted during the 1950s-1980s to prevent **foreign ownership** of domestic assets.
 
 
 
• **Global Context**:
 
 
• While India focused on **domestic markets**, many **East Asian economies** like South Korea adopted **export-oriented growth** during the same period, achieving faster industrial expansion.

questions.question: The Food Corporation of India (FCI) was established in:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1965**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Food Corporation of India (FCI)** is a **Statutory Body** established under the **Food Corporation Act, 1964**, following the recommendations of the **L.K. Jha Committee**.
 
• The organization was officially inaugurated on **January 14, 1965**, with its first regional office established in **Thanjavur**, Tamil Nadu.
 
• Its creation was a strategic response to the severe **Food Grain Scarcity** and price volatility during the mid-1960s, aiming to modernize the country's food management system.
 
• The **FCI** is mandated to fulfill the objectives of the **National Food Policy**, primarily focusing on **Food Security** through procurement, storage, and distribution of essential commodities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Core Objectives**:

 
 
• Implementing **Price Support Operations** to provide **Remunerative Prices** to farmers, preventing distress sales.
 
• Maintaining a **Buffer Stock** of foodgrains (wheat and rice) to ensure national security during crop failures or emergencies.
 
• Facilitating the movement of foodgrains from **Surplus States** to **Deficit States** through the **Public Distribution System (PDS)**.
 
 
 
• **Administrative Setup**:
 
 
• The **FCI** operates under the **Department of Food and Public Distribution** within the **Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution**.
 
• While the initial headquarters were in **Chennai**, the central office was later shifted to **New Delhi** to better coordinate with the central government.
 
• It collaborates with the **Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP)** to execute the **Minimum Support Price (MSP)** regime.
 
 
 
• **Operations**:
 
 
• It acts as the main agency for the **National Food Security Act (NFSA), 2013**, ensuring that highly **Subsidized Foodgrains** reach over 800 million beneficiaries.

questions.question: What is the age group covered under Atal Pension Yojana (APY)?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**18 to 40 years**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Atal Pension Yojana (APY)** was officially launched by Prime Minister **Narendra Modi** on **9th May 2015** in **Kolkata**, replacing the previous **Swavalamban Yojana**.
 
• The scheme is designed to provide **social security** to workers in the **unorganized sector**, ensuring they have a stable income after retirement.
 
• To be eligible for the scheme, an applicant must be an **Indian citizen** within the age bracket of **18 to 40 years**.
 
• The minimum period of contribution by any subscriber under **APY** is **20 years** or more, as the pension benefits begin only after the individual reaches the age of **60**.
 
• It is regulated by the **Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA)** through the **National Pension System (NPS)** framework.
 
• Subscribers are guaranteed a minimum monthly pension of **Rs. 1,000, Rs. 2,000, Rs. 3,000, Rs. 4,000, or Rs. 5,000** based on their contribution amount and age of entry.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Eligibility and Exclusion**:

 
 
• As per the latest amendments effective from **October 1, 2022**, any citizen who is or has been an **income tax payer** is not eligible to join the **Atal Pension Yojana**.
 
• A valid **savings bank account** and a registered **mobile number** are mandatory requirements for enrollment.
 
 
 
• **Death Benefits**:
 
 
• If the subscriber dies, the **spouse** is eligible to receive the same pension amount until their death.
 
• After the demise of both the subscriber and the spouse, the entire **pension corpus** accumulated till age 60 is returned to the **nominee**.
 
 
 
• **Payment Frequency**:
 
 
• Subscribers have the flexibility to make contributions on a **monthly**, **quarterly**, or **half-yearly** basis through an **auto-debit** facility from their linked bank accounts.

questions.question: The Western Ghats are also known as:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sahyadri Hills**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Western Ghats**, also known as the **Sahyadri** mountain range, is a continuous chain of mountains running parallel to the **western coast** of the Indian peninsula, stretching over **1,600 kilometers**.
 
• It originates near the border of **Gujarat** and **Maharashtra**, south of the **Tapti River**, and extends through the states of **Goa**, **Karnataka**, **Kerala**, and **Tamil Nadu**, ending at **Swamithoppe** in **Kanyakumari**.
 
• The range covers an area of approximately **160,000 square kilometers** and has an average elevation of about **1,200 meters** (**3,900 feet**).
 
• In **Maharashtra** and **Northern Karnataka**, the local name for this range is **Sahyadri**, which translates to the **Benevolent Mountains**.
 
• It is one of the world's **eight hottest hotspots** of biological diversity and was declared a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** in **2012** due to its unique biophysical and ecological processes.
 
• The **Western Ghats** act as a major geographical barrier, intercepting the moisture-laden **Southwest Monsoon** winds, which results in heavy **orographic rainfall** on its western slopes.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Vindhya Range**

 
 
• It is a complex system of mountain ridges, hill ranges, and plateau escarpments in **West-Central India**.
 
• Historically, it is considered the traditional boundary between **North India** (Indo-Gangetic plain) and **South India** (Deccan Plateau).
 
 
 
• **Aravali Hills**
 
 
• One of the **oldest fold mountain** systems in the world, located in the northwestern part of India.
 
• It runs approximately **670 kilometers** in a southwest direction, starting near **Delhi**, passing through southern **Haryana** and **Rajasthan**, and ending in **Gujarat**.
 
 
 
• **Nilgiri Hills**
 
 
• Often called the **Blue Mountains**, they are located at the junction of the **Western Ghats** and the **Eastern Ghats** in **Tamil Nadu**.
 
• The highest point in this range is **Doddabetta Peak**, and the area is famous for its **Shola forests** and large-scale **tea cultivation**.

questions.question: Which trade-related policy reform was introduced in 1991 to stimulate India's export growth?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Economic Liberalization Policy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In **July 1991**, India introduced the **New Economic Policy (NEP)** as a response to a severe **Balance of Payments (BoP)** crisis and dwindling foreign exchange reserves.
 
• The **Economic Liberalization Policy** served as the primary trade-related reform designed to end the **License Raj** and open the Indian economy to international competition.
 
• To boost **export growth**, the government executed a **devaluation of the Indian Rupee** by approximately **18-19 percent**, making Indian goods more price-competitive in the global market.
 
• The reform involved the removal of **Quantitative Restrictions (QRs)** on most manufactured consumer goods and agricultural products to facilitate easier trade flows.
 
• It introduced **Trade Policy Reforms** that shifted India from an **inward-looking** protectionist regime to an **outward-looking** export-oriented framework by drastically reducing **import tariffs**.
 
• The policy aimed at achieving **globalization** by encouraging **Foreign Direct Investment (FDI)** and easing the flow of foreign technology into domestic industrial sectors.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Import Substitution Strategy**:

 
 
• Predominant policy before **1991** aimed at protecting domestic industries.
 
• Focused on **self-reliance** by discouraging imports through high tariffs and strict quotas.
 
 
 
• **Green Revolution Strategy**:
 
 
• Initiated in the mid-**1960s** to achieve food security.
 
• Focused on **High-Yielding Variety (HYV)** seeds, irrigation, and fertilizers, primarily for **wheat** and **rice**, rather than trade liberalization.
 
 
 
• **Structural Adjustment Programs**:
 
 
• Part of the **IMF** and **World Bank** conditions for the 1991 bailout.
 
• Included measures like **privatization**, **fiscal discipline**, and the transition from **FERA** (Foreign Exchange Regulation Act) to **FEMA** (Foreign Exchange Management Act).

questions.question: Which important chieftains dominated the Tamil region during the Sangam Age?

options.text: The Chalukyas, the Cheras and the Mauryas
The Cholas, the Cheras and the Pandyas
The Cholas, the Satavahanas and the Guptas
The Pallavas, the Mauryas and the Nandas

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The Cholas, the Cheras and the Pandyas**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The **Sangam Age** is a significant period in the history of **South India**, primarily dating from **300 BCE to 300 CE**, characterized by the flourishing of Tamil literature and culture.
 
• The region of **Tamilakam** was dominated by three powerful dynasties known as the **Muvendar** (the three crowned kings), consisting of the **Cholas**, the **Cheras**, and the **Pandyas**.&

questions.question: The Mahajanapada of Kasi (Kashi) is related to which present-day city?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Banaras (Varanasi)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Kasi** was one of the most powerful of the **sixteen Mahajanapadas** (Sixteen Great States) that existed in ancient India during the **6th century BCE**.
 
• The capital of this Mahajanapada was **Varanasi**, which took its name from the **Varuna** and **Asi** rivers that flow into the **Ganges**.
 
• In early Buddhist literature like the **Anguttara Nikaya**, Kasi is mentioned at the head of the list of the sixteen Mahajanapadas due to its immense prosperity and cultural significance.
 
• The region was a major center for the production of **cotton** and **silk** textiles, and it was renowned for its high-quality craftsmanship in ancient times.
 
• Historically, Kasi was involved in prolonged conflicts with neighboring kingdoms like **Kosala**, **Magadha**, and **Anga**, eventually being annexed by **Kosala** before becoming part of the **Magadhan Empire**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mathura**:

 
 
• It served as the capital of the **Surasena** Mahajanapada.
 
• It was a vital center for the **Bhakti movement** and is traditionally associated with the deity **Krishna**.
 
 
 
• **Allahabad (Prayagraj)**:
 
 
• This region was closely associated with the **Vatsa** Mahajanapada, which had its capital at **Kaushambi**, located approximately 50 km from the modern city.
 
 
 
• **Jaipur**:
 
 
• The area around modern Jaipur was part of the **Matsya** Mahajanapada, with its capital located at **Viratnagar** (modern Bairat).

questions.question: Who was Swami Vivekananda's guru?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ramakrishna Paramhansa**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Swami Vivekananda**, born as **Narendra Nath Datta**, was the chief disciple of the 19th-century Indian mystic **Ramakrishna Paramhansa**.
 
• The duo first met in **1881** at the **Dakshineshwar Kali Temple**, where Ramakrishna served as a priest and practiced various spiritual paths to realize **God**.
 
• **Ramakrishna Paramhansa** is credited with transforming Vivekananda from a skeptical intellectual into a spiritual leader by answering his profound questions on the existence of the **Divine**.
 
• After the passing of his guru in **1886**, Vivekananda carried forward his teachings, emphasizing **Advaita Vedanta** and the philosophy that 'service to man is service to God'.
 
• To honor his guru's legacy, Vivekananda founded the **Ramakrishna Math** and the **Ramakrishna Mission** in **1897**, focusing on worldwide spiritual and humanitarian work.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Ramanand**:

 
 
• A 14th-century **Bhakti Movement** saint who advocated for social equality and was the guru of famous figures like **Kabir** and **Ravidas**.
 
 
 
• **Adi Shankaracharya**:
 
 
• An 8th-century philosopher and theologian who consolidated the doctrine of **Advaita Vedanta** and established four major **Mathas** in India.
 
 
 
• **Chaitanya Mahaprabhu**:
 
 
• A 15th-century saint from Bengal who founded **Gaudiya Vaishnavism** and popularized the **Bhakti** tradition through **Sankirtana** (communal chanting).
 
 
 
• **Swami Vivekananda's Impact**:
 
 
• He is best known for his iconic speech at the **Parliament of the World's Religions** in **Chicago** in **1893**, where he introduced **Hinduism** to the global stage.

questions.question: Who among the following leaders strongly opposed the partition of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan**, widely known as the **Frontier Gandhi**, was a prominent Pashtun leader who was a lifelong follower of **Mahatma Gandhi** and his philosophy of non-violence.
 
• He founded the **Khudai Khidmatgar** (Servants of God) movement in **1929**, which played a critical role in the Indian independence struggle through non-violent resistance against British rule in the **North-West Frontier Province (NWFP)**.
 
• He was a staunch opponent of the **Two-Nation Theory** and the **Partition of India**, believing that a divided nation would lead to communal disharmony and suffering.
 
• When the **Indian National Congress** eventually accepted the partition plan under the **Mountbatten Plan** of **1947**, he felt deeply betrayed and famously remarked, 'You have thrown us to the wolves,' referring to the abandonment of the Pashtun people to the newly formed state of **Pakistan**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mohammad Ali Jinnah**:

 
 
• The leader of the **All India Muslim League** and the primary advocate for the creation of **Pakistan**; he is regarded as the **Father of the Nation** in Pakistan.
 
 
 
• **Chaudhary Rahmat Ali**:
 
 
• A Pakistani nationalist who is credited with coining the name **'Pakistan'** in his **1933** pamphlet titled **'Now or Never'** while studying at the **University of Cambridge**.
 
 
 
• **Liyakat Ali Khan**:
 
 
• A key leader of the **Muslim League** who supported the partition and went on to become the **first Prime Minister** of **Pakistan** in **1947**.
 
 
 
• **Bharat Ratna**:
 
 
• In recognition of his immense contribution to the freedom struggle and his commitment to **secularism**, **Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan** was awarded India's highest civilian honor, the **Bharat Ratna**, in **1987**.

questions.question: In 2025, IMF in its World Economic Outlook, has projected India's GDP growth at around ____ for 2026.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**6.4%**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In its **World Economic Outlook (WEO)** update released in **January 2025**, the **International Monetary Fund (IMF)** projected that **India's GDP** growth would be **6.4%** for the year **2026**.
 
• This projection indicates that **India** will continue to be one of the fastest-growing **major economies** in the world, maintaining significant momentum despite global economic uncertainties.
 
• The **IMF** attributes this growth trajectory to sustained **domestic demand**, a recovery in **private consumption**, and robust **public infrastructure** spending initiated by the government.
 
• The **6.4%** figure reflects a consolidation phase as the economy stabilizes following the **post-pandemic** surge and adjusts to **global financial conditions** and commodity price fluctuations.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **International Monetary Fund (IMF)**:

 
 
• It was established in **1944** at the **Bretton Woods Conference** and is headquartered in **Washington, D.C.**
 
• The organization consists of **190 member countries** working to foster global **monetary cooperation** and secure **financial stability**.
 
• The **World Economic Outlook** is published twice a year, typically in **April** and **October**, with interim updates in **January** and **July**.
 
 
 
• **Economic Growth Metrics**:
 
 
• **GDP (Gross Domestic Product)** is the total monetary value of all finished goods and services produced within a country's borders in a specific time period.
 
• **Real GDP growth** is a key indicator of **economic health**, as it is adjusted for **inflation** to show the actual increase in production.
 
• Other organizations like the **World Bank** and the **Asian Development Bank (ADB)** also provide annual growth forecasts for the **Indian economy**, which often align closely with **IMF** estimates.
